title: Number of Ways to Earn Points
statement:
An exam has `n` kinds of questions. You get an integer `target` and an array `types` in which `types[i] = [count_i, marks_i]`: kind `i` offers `count_i` questions, and solving any one of them scores `marks_i` points.

Count the ways to score exactly `target` points. Questions of one kind cannot be told apart, so a way is fully described by how many questions of each kind you solve (anything from `0` to `count_i` for kind `i`). Two kinds are different kinds even when their `count` and `marks` are equal. Return the count modulo `10^9 + 7`.
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every combination of how many questions to solve per kind multiplies up to `51^n` choices. But the only thing that matters about the kinds handled so far is the score they add up to. So keep, for every score from `0` to `target`, the number of ways to reach it, and fold in one kind at a time. This is a bounded knapsack: each kind is an item that may be used up to `count` times.

## Approach

1. Let `dp[points]` be the number of ways to score `points` with the kinds seen so far. Before any kind, only `dp[0] = 1`.
2. For each kind `[count, marks]`, visit `points` from `target` down to `1`.
3. Add `dp[points - solved * marks]` for every `solved` from `1` to `count` that fits. Because `points` falls, those smaller entries still hold the values from before this kind, so one kind is never counted twice.
4. Keep every sum modulo `10^9 + 7` and return `dp[target]`.

## Example 1, step by step

`target = 6`. Start with `dp = [1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]`.

- Kind `[6, 1]`: any score up to 6 is reachable in one way, so `dp = [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]`.
- Kind `[3, 2]`: for example `dp[6] = 1 + dp[4] + dp[2] + dp[0] = 4` (solving 0 to 3 of them), giving `dp = [1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4]`.
- Kind `[2, 3]`: `dp[6] = 4 + dp[3] + dp[0] = 4 + 2 + 1 = 7`.

The answer is `7`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(target · Σ count_i), at most about 1000 · 50 · 50 = 2.5 million steps.
- Space: O(target) for the single `dp` row.

## Pitfalls

- Walk `points` downwards. Walking upwards reads entries already updated for the same kind and lets a kind be used more than `count` times.
- Same-kind questions are interchangeable: count how many are solved, not which ones.
- Two entries of `types` with the same values are still separate kinds and are both folded in.
- Take the modulus on every addition so the numbers stay small.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `MOD` | `10^9 + 7` |
| `dp` | `dp[points]`: ways to score exactly `points` with the kinds processed so far |
| `count`, `marks` | how many questions the current kind has and what each is worth |
| `points` | the score being updated |
| `solved` | how many questions of the current kind are used |

narration.2: Counts can grow huge, so every sum is kept modulo 10^9 + 7.
narration.3: dp[points] will hold the number of ways to score exactly points with the kinds seen so far.
narration.4: Before any kind is used, the only reachable score is 0, in one way: solve nothing.
narration.5: Fold in one kind of question at a time.
narration.6: Walk scores downwards so the smaller entries still describe the previous kinds only.
narration.7: Try solving 1, 2, ... questions of this kind, as long as they exist and do not overshoot the score.
narration.8: Every way to reach the remaining score before this kind extends to a way to reach points.
narration.12: After all kinds are folded in, dp[target] counts every way to score exactly target.
